title: PRIMUS: A Pioneering Collection of Open-Source Datasets for Cybersecurity LLM Training
authors: Yao-Ching Yu, Tsun-Han Chiang, Cheng-Wei Tsai, Chien-Ming Huang, Wen-Kwang Tsao (Trend Micro Research)

pages.title: Open datasets for cybersecurity LLM training

blocks.html: General-purpose LLMs underperform on cybersecurity tasks — the domain has its own vocabulary (CVEs, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, attack chain semantics), its own knowledge graph (vulnerability databases, threat intelligence reports), and its own task structure (incident response, malware analysis, log triage).
PRIMUS is a curated, openly-released collection of cybersecurity datasets covering all three stages of LLM adaptation:

items: PRIMUS-SEED — high-quality seed corpus from authoritative sources.
PRIMUS-FineWeb — large-scale pre-training corpus filtered from CommonCrawl using a classifier trained on PRIMUS-SEED.
PRIMUS-Instruct — instruction-tuning data tailored to cybersecurity workflows.
PRIMUS-Reasoning — reasoning-trace data distilled from a teacher model for reflection-style training.

blocks.html: Headline result: continued pre-training on PRIMUS-FineWeb gives a 15.9% improvement on aggregated cybersecurity benchmarks. All datasets are released under the MIT license; classifiers and code under ODC-BY.

items: Recent surveys (Zhang 2024, Xu 2024) show base LLMs trained on web text are systematically weak at cybersecurity tasks despite covering many adjacent domains.
Existing cybersecurity LLM papers (LLaMa-Primus, Lily, CySecBert) all build on private or closed datasets — limiting reproducibility and stalling community progress.
Other technical domains (medicine, code, math) have benefited enormously from public domain-specific corpora. Cybersecurity has not had its equivalent until now.

blocks.html: PRIMUS-SEED is the curated foundation — scraped from authoritative cybersecurity sources (CISA, NIST, MITRE, security vendor advisories, well-known security blogs, conference proceedings).

Source documents are converted from HTML to clean Markdown using dom-to-semantic-markdown, then deduplicated and lightly filtered. Result: a smaller but very high-quality corpus that's used both as direct training data and as positive examples for the classifier that filters the much larger FineWeb step.

The scale problem: PRIMUS-SEED alone isn't large enough to meaningfully shift a base model. The solution: train a classifier on PRIMUS-SEED (positive class) and random CommonCrawl text (negative class), then run it across CommonCrawl/FineWeb to extract every document that looks cybersecurity-relevant.
This is the same fastText-classifier-on-Common-Crawl recipe used for code and math corpora — applied here to cybersecurity. The yield is on the order of billions of tokens of in-domain text.

PRIMUS-Instruct: instruction-response pairs covering common cybersecurity workflows — explaining a CVE, classifying a log entry, walking through an attack chain, answering policy questions. Seeded from real expert content and expanded with templates.

PRIMUS-Reasoning: longer-form reasoning traces (chain-of-thought style) distilled from a strong teacher model on cybersecurity problems. Intended for reflection-style fine-tuning where the model is taught to think step by step before answering.

items: Continued pre-training on PRIMUS-FineWeb gives Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct a 15.9% lift on aggregated cybersecurity benchmarks while retaining general-instruction-following capability.
Instruction tuning with PRIMUS-Instruct gives a 15.8% gain on security certification benchmarks.
Reasoning distillation with PRIMUS-Reasoning further improves multi-step reasoning tasks where chain-of-thought helps.

blocks.html: Importantly, the gains stack — continued pre-training plus instruction tuning plus reasoning distillation gives larger total improvements than any single stage alone.

pages.title: Open data as a foundation for cybersecurity AI

blocks.html: PRIMUS is the first openly licensed, comprehensive cybersecurity LLM training corpus spanning pre-training, instruction tuning, and reasoning. The paper argues this is the first piece of common infrastructure the community has needed to make cybersecurity-LLM research reproducible and cumulative.

Future directions called out: multilingual cybersecurity data, more recent threat intelligence, evaluation benchmarks specific to red-team and blue-team workflows, and safety considerations specific to releasing security-capable models openly.
